questions.stem: The marginal propensity to consume (MPC) is:
options: the share of each extra dollar of income that households save
the total consumption spending of all households in a year
the share of each extra dollar of income that is spent on consumption
the share of total income that households spend on consumption
questions.explanation: The MPC measures how consumption changes when income changes: change in consumption divided by change in income. The share of total income spent is the average propensity to consume.

questions.stem: In the simple Keynesian model, if the marginal propensity to consume is 0.8, the marginal propensity to save is:
questions.explanation: Each extra dollar of income is either spent or saved in the simple model, so MPC + MPS = 1 and MPS = 1 - 0.8 = 0.2. The value 5 is the multiplier, not the MPS.

questions.stem: If the marginal propensity to consume is 0.75, the value of the simple Keynesian multiplier is:
questions.explanation: The multiplier is 1 / (1 - MPC) = 1 / 0.25 = 4. Dividing 1 by the MPC itself gives 1.33, a common slip.

questions.stem: The marginal propensity to save in an economy is 0.2. Using the simple Keynesian model, the multiplier is:
questions.explanation: The multiplier equals 1 / MPS, so 1 / 0.2 = 5. An injection of spending would raise national income by five times the initial amount in this simple model.

questions.stem: The government increases its spending by $10 billion. The marginal propensity to consume is 0.6. Using the simple Keynesian multiplier, by how much will national income eventually rise?
options: $25 billion
$16 billion
$6 billion
$60 billion
questions.explanation: The multiplier is 1 / (1 - 0.6) = 1 / 0.4 = 2.5, so income rises by $10 billion x 2.5 = $25 billion. Adding the first round of extra consumption ($6 billion) to the $10 billion gives $16 billion, which ignores the later rounds.

questions.stem: The government wants national income to rise by $30 billion. If the marginal propensity to consume is 0.8, what initial injection of spending is needed, using the simple multiplier?
options: $37.5 billion
$6 billion
$24 billion
$150 billion
questions.explanation: The multiplier is 1 / (1 - 0.8) = 5, so the injection needed is $30 billion / 5 = $6 billion. Multiplying $30 billion by the MPC gives $24 billion, which confuses the multiplier with the MPC.

questions.stem: The multiplier effect occurs because:
options: prices rise by the same proportion as the initial increase in spending
businesses always invest every dollar that households choose to save
one person's spending becomes another's income, part of which is spent again
the government prints extra money each time households increase their saving
questions.explanation: An injection becomes income for workers and firms, who spend part of it, creating further income in successive rounds. Each round is smaller because part of the income leaks out of the flow.

questions.stem: In a real open economy with taxes, the multiplier is smaller than the simple 1 / (1 - MPC) value mainly because:
options: part of each round of extra income leaks into taxation and imports as well as saving
governments always cut their spending as soon as national income starts to rise
households spend more of each extra dollar of income than the simple model assumes
exports rise automatically each time domestic income rises in the economy
questions.explanation: The simple multiplier counts only saving as a leakage. In practice, taxes and spending on imports also withdraw income from each round, so the total effect on domestic income is smaller.

questions.stem: Households become worried about job security and decide to save a larger share of each extra dollar they earn. The likely effect on the multiplier is that it:
options: becomes smaller, so a given injection raises national income by less
becomes larger, so a given injection raises national income by more
stays the same, because the multiplier depends only on interest rates
becomes negative, so any injection reduces national income instead
questions.explanation: A higher MPS means a lower MPC, so less of each round is re-spent and the multiplier 1 / MPS falls. Fiscal stimulus is therefore less powerful when households are cautious.

questions.stem: A household with an income of $80,000 spends $64,000 on consumption. Its average propensity to consume is:
questions.explanation: The average propensity to consume is total consumption divided by total income: 64,000 / 80,000 = 0.8. Its average propensity to save is therefore 0.2.

questions.stem: A household's income rises from $60,000 to $70,000, and its consumption rises from $54,000 to $60,000. Its marginal propensity to consume is:
questions.explanation: The MPC is the change in consumption divided by the change in income: 6,000 / 10,000 = 0.6. The figures 0.9 and 0.86 are the average propensities to consume before and after the rise, and 0.4 is the MPS.

questions.stem: The RBA raises the cash rate target from 3.85 per cent to 4.10 per cent. This is an increase of:
options: 25 basis points
2.5 basis points
250 basis points
6.5 basis points
questions.explanation: One basis point is one-hundredth of a percentage point. A rise of 0.25 percentage points is therefore 25 basis points.

questions.stem: The unemployment rate rises from 4.0 per cent to 4.5 per cent. Which statement is correct?
options: It rose by 12.5 percentage points, an increase of 0.5 per cent
It rose by 5 basis points, an increase of 12.5 per cent
It rose by 0.5 percentage points, an increase of 12.5 per cent
It rose by 0.5 per cent, an increase of 0.5 percentage points
questions.explanation: The difference between two rates is measured in percentage points: 4.5 - 4.0 = 0.5. As a proportion of the starting rate, that is 0.5 / 4.0 x 100 = 12.5 per cent. 0.5 percentage points equals 50 basis points, not 5.

questions.stem: A home loan charges 6.0 per cent interest a year while inflation is 3.5 per cent. The approximate real interest rate is:
options: 9.5 per cent
6.0 per cent
1.7 per cent
2.5 per cent
questions.explanation: The real interest rate is approximately the nominal rate minus inflation: 6.0 - 3.5 = 2.5 per cent. It shows the true cost of borrowing after allowing for the fall in money's purchasing power.

questions.stem: Stagflation describes an economy experiencing:
options: rapid growth together with low inflation and low unemployment
a budget deficit together with a current account surplus
high inflation together with high unemployment and weak growth
falling prices together with strong growth and low unemployment
questions.explanation: Stagflation combines stagnant output and rising unemployment with high inflation, usually after a fall in aggregate supply such as an oil price shock. It is hard to treat because policies that reduce inflation tend to worsen unemployment.

questions.stem: In the aggregate demand and aggregate supply model, the equilibrium price level and level of real output are found where:
options: the aggregate supply curve meets the horizontal axis of the diagram
injections into the circular flow equal government spending alone
the aggregate demand curve intersects the aggregate supply curve
the aggregate demand curve meets the vertical axis of the diagram
questions.explanation: Equilibrium occurs where total planned spending equals total planned output. On the diagram that is the intersection of AD and AS, giving the price level on the vertical axis and real GDP on the horizontal axis.

questions.stem: A rise in the general price level, with nothing else changing, causes:
options: a shift of the aggregate demand curve to the left as confidence falls
a movement along the aggregate demand curve to a lower real output demanded
a shift of the aggregate demand curve to the right as spending increases
a shift of the aggregate supply curve to the left as costs increase
questions.explanation: A change in the price level itself moves the economy along the existing AD curve. AD shifts only when a non-price factor changes, such as interest rates, confidence or the exchange rate.

questions.stem: In the long run, an increase in aggregate demand with no change in the economy's productive capacity is most likely to:
options: shift the long-run aggregate supply curve to the right over time
raise the price level but leave real output at its potential level
raise real output permanently with no change in the price level
lower both the price level and real output below their potential
questions.explanation: Long-run aggregate supply is fixed by the economy's resources and technology, so it is drawn vertical at potential output. Extra demand then adds to prices rather than lasting output.

questions.stem: The economy is operating close to full capacity when a surge in business investment shifts aggregate demand to the right. On a short-run AS curve that becomes steeper near capacity, the most likely result is:
options: a large rise in the price level and only a small rise in real output
a large rise in real output and no change in the price level
a fall in the price level and a large rise in real output
a fall in real output and a large fall in the price level
questions.explanation: Near capacity, firms cannot expand output easily, so extra spending bids up prices. With plenty of spare capacity, the same rise in AD would mostly raise real output.

questions.stem: Which is a structural, rather than cyclical, factor affecting aggregate supply?
options: A short-lived fall in consumer confidence
A temporary drop in business investment
A seasonal rise in demand before Christmas
The long-term ageing of the population
questions.explanation: Structural factors change the economy's productive capacity over the long term, such as demographics, technology and skills. Swings in confidence, investment and seasonal demand are cyclical and affect demand rather than capacity.

questions.stem: As an economy recovers from a recession, it moves from a point inside its production possibility curve to a point on it. Compared with an outward shift of the curve, this movement represents:
options: a fall in productivity, as resources move to less efficient uses
an increase in the economy's natural resources and population
using idle resources, rather than an increase in productive capacity
an increase in productive capacity, rather than using idle resources
questions.explanation: A move from inside to the curve reflects re-employing unemployed resources, a cyclical recovery. An outward shift of the curve reflects growth in productive capacity, which shifts long-run AS to the right.

questions.stem: Which of the following is usually classed as a coincident indicator?
options: Real GDP
Building approvals
The unemployment rate
Consumer sentiment
questions.explanation: Coincident indicators move at the same time as overall economic activity, such as output and retail sales. Building approvals and sentiment tend to lead the cycle, while unemployment tends to lag it.

questions.stem: Growth in wages is usually classed as a lagging indicator because:
options: wages always change several months before the economy turns up or down
wages are fixed by law and do not respond to economic conditions
wages move at exactly the same time as total output in the economy
wages are set in agreements that adjust only after labour market conditions change
questions.explanation: Wage agreements and awards are reviewed periodically, so wages respond to tighter or looser labour markets with a delay. That makes wages growth confirm a turning point after it has happened.

questions.stem: Share market prices are often treated as a leading indicator because they:
options: are set by the Reserve Bank to signal changes in monetary policy
reflect investors' expectations of future profits and economic conditions
are calculated from last year's company profits after they are published
move only after the unemployment rate has changed for several quarters
questions.explanation: Share prices are based on expected future earnings, so they tend to move before activity turns. They can also give false signals, which is why several leading indicators are used together.

questions.stem: Over two quarters, real GDP grows by 0.2 per cent and then falls by 0.1 per cent, unemployment is rising, inflation is easing, and building approvals have risen for three months in a row. The economy is most likely:
options: in the middle of a strong expansion phase
in a boom, with very low unemployment
near the trough, with leading signs of a recovery
at the peak, with inflationary pressure building
questions.explanation: Weak output, rising unemployment and easing inflation suggest a contraction at or near its low point. Rising building approvals, a leading indicator, suggest activity may soon pick up.

questions.stem: The CPI rises from 128.0 to 132.48 over a year. The rate of inflation is:
options: 32.48 per cent
3.5 per cent
4.48 per cent
3.4 per cent
questions.explanation: Inflation = (132.48 - 128.0) / 128.0 x 100 = 4.48 / 128.0 x 100 = 3.5 per cent. The change of 4.48 index points is not itself a percentage.

questions.stem: In an economy, 14.1 million people are employed, 0.6 million are unemployed and the civilian population aged 15 and over is 21.0 million. The unemployment rate is about:
options: 70.0 per cent
4.1 per cent
4.3 per cent
2.9 per cent
questions.explanation: The labour force is 14.1 + 0.6 = 14.7 million, so the unemployment rate is 0.6 / 14.7 x 100, about 4.1 per cent. Dividing by employment alone gives 4.3 per cent, and 70 per cent is the participation rate.

questions.stem: Real GDP rises from $1,950 billion to $2,008.5 billion over a year. The rate of real economic growth is:
options: 58.5 per cent
3.0 per cent
5.85 per cent
2.9 per cent
questions.explanation: Growth = (2,008.5 - 1,950) / 1,950 x 100 = 58.5 / 1,950 x 100 = 3.0 per cent. Dividing by the new value instead gives about 2.9 per cent.

questions.stem: A limitation of the unemployment rate as a measure of spare capacity in the labour market is that it:
options: counts people who work only one hour a week as unemployed
includes retirees and full-time students in the labour force
is published only once every five years with the Census
leaves out underemployed workers and the hidden unemployed
questions.explanation: Part-time workers who want more hours are counted as employed, and discouraged job seekers are outside the labour force. Measures such as underutilisation give a fuller picture.

questions.stem: The first estimate of quarterly GDP is often revised later. This affects the reliability of GDP as an indicator because:
options: GDP is measured only in nominal terms and cannot be adjusted for inflation
revisions mean GDP can never be compared between two different years
early figures rely on incomplete data, so the picture of the economy can change
the ABS changes the definition of GDP each quarter to suit government policy
questions.explanation: Initial estimates are based on partial survey and tax data, and later information can alter growth rates noticeably. Policymakers must allow for the risk that early readings are wrong.

questions.stem: The original Phillips curve showed:
options: a direct relationship between government spending and the tax rate
an inverse relationship between unemployment and the rate of wage inflation
a direct relationship between economic growth and the current account deficit
an inverse relationship between interest rates and the exchange rate
questions.explanation: A.W. Phillips found, using British data, that wage inflation tended to be higher when unemployment was low. Later versions relate unemployment to price inflation.

questions.stem: According to the short-run Phillips curve, policy that pushes unemployment well below the NAIRU is most likely to:
options: cause sustained deflation
raise the rate of inflation
lower the rate of inflation
leave inflation unchanged
questions.explanation: When the labour market tightens, firms compete for workers and wages and prices rise faster. The short-run curve shows this trade-off between lower unemployment and higher inflation.

questions.stem: Many economists draw the long-run Phillips curve as a vertical line at the NAIRU. This implies that:
options: lower unemployment can be bought permanently by accepting a higher rate of inflation
unemployment always falls to zero in the long run if inflation is kept stable
there is no lasting trade-off, as expectations adjust and unemployment returns to the NAIRU
inflation can be kept at any level the government chooses without affecting output
questions.explanation: Once workers and firms expect higher inflation, they build it into wages and prices, so unemployment drifts back to its natural rate with inflation now higher. Lasting falls in unemployment need lower structural unemployment, not more demand.

questions.stem: A sharp rise in world oil prices brings both higher inflation and higher unemployment. On a Phillips curve diagram this is best shown as:
options: a movement up along the short-run Phillips curve
an outward shift of the short-run Phillips curve
a movement down along the short-run Phillips curve
an inward shift of the long-run Phillips curve
questions.explanation: A movement along the curve trades one goal against the other. When both inflation and unemployment rise together, as in a supply shock causing stagflation, the whole short-run curve has shifted outwards.

questions.stem: The RBA raises interest rates to bring inflation back to target, accepting that unemployment will rise for a time. This is an example of:
options: a supply-side policy aimed at lowering the NAIRU
an intertemporal trade-off between short-term costs and long-term stability
a policy with no conflict between the macroeconomic objectives
an automatic stabiliser operating through the federal budget
questions.explanation: Tightening policy costs some output and jobs now in return for low and stable inflation later, which supports sustainable growth. Trade-offs over time like this are central to judging economic management.
